name: Chin, Bawm
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: 3. STRESS Stress is not phonemic and in general is distributed evenly on the syllables. Northern Bawm has a tendency to stress the last syllable of polysyllabic words. The southern dialect joins this tendency in loan words, where the last syllable always carries tone 2

tone_statements.citation: Löffler, Lorenz G. 2002. The tonal system of Chin final stops. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(2): 123-153. DOI 10.15144/LTBA-25.2.123.
tone_statements.quote: Tones to be reconstructed: 1) low, 2) high. ... Even though Lushai has 4, Lai, Maraa and Tedim have 3, and Bawm has but 2 tones, in the overwhelming number of cognates the tone remains basically the same. ... As we can see, only Lushai has 4 tones; Tedim, Lai and Maara have 3; Bawm has merely 2. ... In Bawm there is a very conspicuous high-low falling tone, but I have not discussed it, since it is nothing but a conditioned “allotone” of t1 (Loffler 1972).
tone_statements.locator: p. 123 ('Introduction: sources and problems') and p. 126
tone_statements.summary: Bawm has two tones, t1 low and t2 high (Lushai t3 and t4 merged with t1 in Bawm); a conspicuous high-low falling pitch is a conditioned allotone of t1; first-position syllables are mostly level.

tone_statements.citation: Namkung, Ju (1996). Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages. Berkeley: Center for Southeast Asia Studies. xxvii+507 pp.
tone_statements.quote: TONES / Northern Dialect / ma (1) low / ma (2) medium or rising / ma (3) high / Southern Dialect / ma (1) flat / ma (2) raised / • Tones are not consistently indicated. / • In the northern dialect, pitch is grammatically determined and is not generally indicated. / • In the southern dialect, the two tones are phonemic in nouns and verbs. There is also a third falling tone which is an intonation contour, and pitch levels associated with grammatical particles.

audit.recode_to: No class change: keep fixed-strict (final) final stress, counts as exceptionless (the strict set), in the dominant set. The only edit owed is to populate the record's empty caution field with the fences the source carries: (i) evenness/non-phonemic ('Stress is not phonemic and in general is distributed evenly on the syllables', p.13); (ii) hedge ('a tendency'); (iii) dialect scope (rule = Northern Bawm; Southern Bawm shows it only in loans, final syllable pitch level 2); (iv) tone/pitch (S. Bawm two phonemic tones, p.7/p.14; N. Bawm three grammatically distributed pitch levels, p.13 sec. 5.1). A register change, if the compilers wants one, must be ruled for the whole parity class (Tonkawa, Olo, Alawa, Anem, Awtuw, Talaud..), not for Bawm alone.

sources.quote: No statement on stress placement. Reads Reichle 1981:13-15 as: Southern Bawm has a two-way lexical tone distinction (Flat vs Raised); Northern Bawm 'has a three-way contrast between L, M (or Rising), and H pitches, with their distribution, in part, lexically constrained' (fn.3: L in nouns/verbs, H in adverbial/adnominal/phrase-type markers, Rise in demonstrative/emphatic particles); lists N. Bawm in the SC tone-inventory table. I.e. the tone literature treats both dialects as pitch/tone systems, not stress systems.
sources.locator: p.37 with fn.2-3; pp.39-40 (pitch-inventory table row 'N. Bawm.. Reichle 1981')
sources.note: Current secondary reading of Reichle 1981:13-15; treats Northern Bawm as a three-way pitch-contrast system, which bears on whether 'fixed-strict final stress' is the right class.
